strengths: Elegant and novel conceptual connection: The paper beautifully bridges multicalibration (a notion from algorithmic fairness) with decision-making/optimization under imperfect predictions, showing how post-processing a predictor can make a standard optimization pipeline competitive with any decision rule.

Simplicity and clarity of the core results: Theorem 1 and its proof are remarkably clean, using the definition of multicalibration to elegantly sandwich the expected utility of the optimal decision rule.

Instance-dependent sample complexity: The sample complexity bounds scale with the mean squared error (MSE) of the initial predictor. This means that if the starting black-box model is already reasonably good, the refinement requires significantly fewer samples.
Broad applicability: The framework is shown to be flexible and extends naturally to other linear optimization problems, such as matroids, best-action selection, and learning with rejection.
weaknesses: High polynomial sample complexity: The sample complexity has a dependency on $n^8$ (or $n^6$ with a good starting predictor) where $n$ is the number of nodes in the graph. While theoretically polynomial, this high exponent makes the approach impractical for graphs of even moderate size (e.g., $n = 50$).

Reliance on the CHECK oracle: The algorithm assumes access to a CHECK oracle (Definition 2). While this is standard in the multicalibration literature, implementing this oracle efficiently in practice for large or complex decision classes $C$ can be a significant computational hurdle.

Lack of empirical validation: The paper is purely theoretical. While the theoretical contribution is solid, simple illustrative simulations comparing the proposed method against empirical risk minimization over the class $C$ would have greatly enhanced the paper and shed light on the tightness of the sample complexity bounds.

strengths: Conceptual Novelty: The paper successfully bridges algorithmic fairness (multicalibration) and combinatorial optimization with predictions, showing how post-processing via multicalibration guarantees near-optimal downstream decisions.
Simplicity and Elegance: The proof of Theorem 1 is remarkably clean, elegant, and easy to follow, yet it establishes a strong and general guarantee.

Modularity: The pipeline is highly modular. The decision class $\mathcal{C}$ is only required during the offline calibration phase. In the online test phase, one only needs to run the standard exact algorithm (e.g., Edmonds' algorithm) on the adjusted weights.

Fine-Grained Sample Complexity: The sample complexity bounds scale with the mean-squared error $r$ of the initial predictor, reflecting the intuitive fact that better initial predictors require fewer samples to calibrate.
weaknesses: Lack of Empirical Evaluation: The paper is entirely theoretical. Since the motivation is highly practical (e.g., industry pipelines using ML predictors), some experimental validation on synthetic or real-world matching datasets would greatly strengthen the work and show the practical viability of the calibration algorithm.

High Worst-Case Sample Complexity: The worst-case sample complexity scales as $O(n^8/\varepsilon^4)$ when $r = O(n^2)$. This is extremely high and may limit applicability to large-scale graphs unless $r$ is exceptionally small. A discussion on how to improve this exponent or whether it is tight would be highly valuable.

Finiteness of the Decision Class: The analysis currently assumes a finite family of decision rules $\mathcal{C}$. Discussing how to extend this to infinite classes of decision rules (e.g., via VC dimension or covering numbers) would make the framework much more general.

strengths: The paper is very well-written, clearly organized, and easy to follow.
The conceptual connection between algorithmic fairness (multicalibration) and decision-making under predictive uncertainty in combinatorial optimization is neat and intuitive.
The proposed framework is versatile and can be generalized to other linear optimization problems, such as matroids and learning with rejection.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The main theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) is a straightforward application of the weighted multicalibration framework from Gopalan et al. (2022b). The proof is very simple and relies on direct definitions, which limits the technical depth of the paper.

Impractical sample complexity: The worst-case sample complexity is O(n^8 / epsilon^4), and even under optimistic assumptions where the initial predictor's MSE is O(epsilon^2), it remains O(n^8 / epsilon^2). For any realistic graph size (e.g., n = 100), this requires an astronomical number of samples, making the method highly impractical.

Lack of empirical evaluation: The paper is purely theoretical. Given the practical motivation highlighted in the introduction, an empirical study is highly desirable to show whether the method can run efficiently in practice despite the pessimistic theoretical bounds.

Weak justification over the ERM baseline: The paper acknowledges that a simple baseline (estimating the expected performance of each decision rule and selecting the best) has a much better sample complexity of O(n^4 / (epsilon^2) * log|C|). The proposed benefits of multicalibration (such as having a single algorithm at test time or improving the predictor in the MSE sense) do not seem to justify the massive polynomial increase in sample complexity.
